summary: Describes how to carry redundant copies of audio data in RTP packets, so that if a packet is lost the sound can be rebuilt from a later one. A packet holds the current audio plus a lower-quality copy of earlier audio. This helps voice calls survive packet loss on the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2198 defines an RTP format that sends the current audio together with copies of earlier audio. If a packet is lost, a receiver may recover its audio from a later packet.

subtitle: A payload format that carries copies of earlier audio so a receiver can recover from some packet losses.

tldr.problem: Lost packets can make speech difficult to understand, even when the packet-loss rate is low.
tldr.mechanism: The format places the current audio and one or more lower-bandwidth copies of earlier audio in one RTP payload. Headers identify each block's payload type, time offset, and length.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can use a later packet to reconstruct audio from a lost packet, when the loss pattern allows it. RFC 2198 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6354.

today: RFC 2198 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6354.

sections.title: Redundancy for Lost Audio Packets
sections.content:
RFC 2198 defines a payload format for redundant audio in version 2 of the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). Its main motivation is audio conferencing over networks where packets can be lost. The RFC notes that even low loss rates can disrupt speech intelligibility.

A later packet can carry redundant audio for an earlier time interval. If a packet is lost, the receiver may reconstruct its missing audio from redundancy in following packets, provided the average number of consecutive losses is small.
sections.plainLanguage: A later audio packet can include audio data from an earlier time. That extra data may let the receiver restore sound when an earlier packet is lost.

sections.title: One Payload Container for Several Encodings
sections.content:
A redundant packet must carry a primary audio encoding and one or more redundant encodings. Each block needs an encoding identifier, a length, and a way to identify its time interval. RFC 2198 chooses one payload type to mark the packet as a container for several payload blocks.

The RFC rejects a header extension as the preferred approach because its extension and padding add overhead and it does not naturally support several redundant encodings. Assigning a separate payload type to every encoding combination also scales poorly when packets carry multiple redundancy blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: One RTP payload type marks a packet that contains several audio blocks. Each block has a small header that tells the receiver how to interpret it.

sections.title: Headers for Redundant Audio Blocks
sections.content:
The RTP header fields describe the primary block. After the RTP header come headers for the redundant blocks and then a header for the primary block. Each redundant-block header is 32 bits: a flag indicating whether another header follows, a 7-bit payload type, a 14-bit timestamp offset, and a 10-bit block length in bytes.

The timestamp offset is unsigned and is subtracted from the RTP timestamp to identify the earlier time represented by that redundant block. The primary block's final header is only 8 bits because its timestamp and length can be derived from the RTP header and packet length. Data blocks follow their headers in order, without padding or delimiters between blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each redundant block has a label for its encoding, its earlier time, and its size. The primary audio block comes last, and its header is shorter.

sections.title: Describing Redundancy with SDP
sections.content:
An RTP profile or a dynamic payload type assignment identifies the redundant payload format. When Session Description Protocol (SDP) is used, the codec name for this format is red. The media description lists the payload types the receiver must be ready to handle, including those used by redundant blocks.

To describe which formats a sender uses for the primary and redundant blocks, SDP uses an fmtp attribute containing a slash-separated list of RTP payload types. Each format listed there must also be allowed by the media description.
sections.plainLanguage: The SDP description tells both sides which audio formats are allowed. It can also list which format is primary and which formats provide redundancy.

sections.title: Limits, Security, and Status
sections.content:
Redundant blocks do not preserve the RTP marker bit or the CSRC information for the primary block. The RFC also warns that adding too much redundancy can increase congestion and packet loss, worsening the problem the format aims to reduce. The RTP security considerations apply; encryption across a stream boundary can prevent sending a redundant copy of the last packet under the appropriate key.

RFC 2198 is a Proposed Standard. Unit metadata lists RFC 6354 as an update.
sections.plainLanguage: Redundancy uses extra network capacity, so too much can cause more packet loss. Some RTP header information from the primary block is not copied to redundant blocks.
